As vibe coding (using AI prompts to write programs) grows in popularity, the number of new apps submitted to the App Store has surged, doubling in the first half of 2026—though downloads grew by only 2%. Here is the full summary.

New app submissions have risen sharply, but downloads lag far behind

The New York Times published a report today, citing the latest data from Sensor Tower, pointing out that although new app submissions to the App Store doubled in the first half of 2026, downloads rose by only 2%.

The report also focused on two developers who have been continuously releasing vibe-coded apps on the App Store: Marco Pérez plans to quit his job at JPMorgan next month to work full-time on app development; David Svensson, on the other hand, has launched 11 niche apps over the past five months, treating vibe coding as a hobby rather than a business.

Excerpts from the report are as follows:

Pérez is a Chicago-based software engineer who had never developed a mobile app before. He spent five weeks during the winter researching "vibe coding" AI tools to build prototypes, then another two weeks preparing to submit to the App Store. His app InfoDrizzle performed fairly well, accumulating 1,300 downloads to date and earning roughly US$500 in profit. Pérez's next app proved even more popular. He spent about a week in May launching Stampa, a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps, which has since been downloaded 20,000 times, generating around US$3,000 in profit.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian, responding to the New York Times, mentioned another issue arising from the surge in submissions: earlier reports had noted that the App Store's review process is under enormous pressure as a result.

Ajemian said: "Apple has consistently been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours", and added that Apple "welcomes a new generation of developers using the latest tools to build and launch apps at an unprecedented pace".

He also pointed out that all apps "whether developed through vibe coding or not, must meet the same high standards of quality, privacy, and security that users have always relied upon".
